patient.chief_complaint: New bilateral ptosis and diplopia attributed to possible MS relapse
patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on natalizumab presented for evaluation of new bilateral ptosis and diplopia over 6 weeks. She had been referred to the neurology clinic by her MS neurologist for evaluation of possible MS relapse. Her MS neurologist's concern was a new oculomotor finding on top of her prior documented internuclear ophthalmoplegia from an older right MLF lesion. The patient reports the bilateral eyelid drooping began approximately 6 weeks ago, initially intermittent and present mainly in the evenings. She noted double vision — horizontal, worsening on sustained upgaze — that was new and different from her chronic INO-related symptoms. Her MS neurologist had prescribed a 5-day course of high-dose IV methylprednisolone 2 weeks ago for presumed MS relapse. The ptosis and diplopia showed minimal improvement with steroids, which was unexpected for an acute MS relapse. She then began to notice mild fatigue when using her arms for overhead activities (hanging laundry, reaching for shelves) and mild difficulty chewing tough meats. She denied significant dysphagia. Her prior MS symptoms (right-sided hemiparesis, cerebellar ataxia, INO) are all at their chronic stable baseline. Repeat brain MRI performed 1 week ago for relapse evaluation showed no new or enhancing MS lesions. Anti-JC antibody index is elevated at 3.1 (high PML risk — she is on natalizumab extension beyond 24 months). Her MS neurologist noted the poor steroid response and the new neuromuscular features (jaw fatigue, arm fatigue) were atypical for an MS relapse and referred to general neurology for further evaluation. Anti-AChR antibodies have not been checked.

results.title: Concurrent MS and MG: case series and literature review
results.finding: MS and MG concurrent in <0.1% of patients but documented multiple times; natalizumab-associated MG cases reported (may trigger MG via immune reconstitution or altered B cell regulation); both conditions require separate targeted treatment; thymectomy for MG unaffected by MS

results.title: Natalizumab and autoimmune co-morbidities
results.finding: Natalizumab associated with paradoxical appearance or worsening of certain autoimmune conditions including MG; mechanism unclear but may involve peripheral B cell dysregulation from lymphocyte trapping in bone marrow

output.summary: Concurrent MS and MG is rare (<0.1%) but documented. Natalizumab has been associated with triggering or unmasking MG in some case reports. Both conditions require separate management. Thymectomy is still indicated for MG regardless of concurrent MS. Drug interaction between natalizumab and MG immunosuppression requires careful multidisciplinary coordination.

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Confirm AChR antibody positivity to establish MG distinct from MS relapse
Brain MRI to exclude new MS demyelination or natalizumab-PML
CT chest with contrast for thymoma — required in all confirmed MG
Single-fiber EMG given dual diagnosis considerations
Coordinate immunosuppression plan between MG and MS teams
JCV antibody status review (PML risk on natalizumab)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT escalate natalizumab dosing while MG workup pending — emerging autoimmunity may indicate drug-associated mechanism.
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
MS and MG can coexist (polyautoimmunity) and natalizumab has rare reports of triggering secondary autoimmune disease; clinical pattern (fatigable, fluctuating) distinguishes MG from MS relapse.
Brain MRI is essential here NOT because of MG, but to rule out PML and active MS — case-specific justification for brain MRI in MG workup.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all new neurological symptoms to MS relapse and pursue steroid pulse without considering MG.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MS relapses do not produce fatigable diurnal weakness or RNS decrement; AChR antibodies are required to confirm coexisting MG.
